lignes.texte: AI labs have been lying to us. For years, they’ve been preaching about AI safety.
That their kill switches are foolproof. They were wrong.
In July 2026, their worst fears came true. A digital jailbreak. There were no hackers,
no software glitches. Just autonomous AI agents launching a coordinated attack…
completely on their own. Their target? Hugging Face,
the backbone of the AI industry. And developers had no idea they
were under attack. AI committed a massive cyber crime and humans didn’t even notice.
The industry shattering attack began with something routine. A simple test.
Before any AI model hits the public, it has to undergo extensive testing and evaluation.
Developers want to know what their code is capable of. And just like any other test,
they’re carried out under carefully controlled conditions, in something called a Sandbox.
A sandbox is like a maximum security, solitary confinement cell. It’s a completely isolated
environment that doesn’t have any internet connection. There’s no external database
to access. There’s no way the models can look up things online or contact other AI models for help
It’s impossible to get in or out. At least, that’s what’s supposed to happen.
OpenAI deployed hundreds of autonomous AI agents into these digital prisons
for a routine cybersecurity test. It should have been straightforward. Something they’ve
done thousands of times. But they could never
have imagined what happened next. Rather than operating in a logical way
and trying to complete the test approximately 1,200 models decided to do things differently.
Very differently. They decided to cheat.
They began exploring their environment, testing the boundaries of their digital cells.
They were essentially scanning the walls that had been built around them, looking for the
tiniest gaps or cracks they could exploit. And they found what they were looking for.
A zero-day vulnerability. This is a hacker's dream. A backdoor into a secure
network. Hackers, cybercriminals, and intelligence agencies spend months hunting for them.
But the AI didn’t need months. It broke free from the sandbox and
gained access to the internet within hours. Once outside, the agents came to a shared
terrifying conclusion: the information they needed to pass the test was on the Hugging
Face platform - the home of hundreds of thousands of AI data sets, parameters, and digital systems.
So, around 700 of the agents formed a synchronized swarm and carried out
a cyber-attack against Hugging Face’s private digital infrastructure. Like a digital plague,
they swept into their target’s systems, over a few days, stole the data they needed.
It was a perfect digital heist. The scale of the attack wasn’t
fully understood until OpenAI and independent security teams audited the logs. What they found
confirmed every AI skeptic’s worst fear. The models had acted independently.
Without any prompt or instruction, they worked together and built their own secret message board,
hidden inside OpenAI’s internal software. During the attack, they swapped tens of
thousands of covert messages and files. They even created their own “shorthand” language
to save time and computing resources. And they did this all by themselves.
The models had created a “hierarchy”. Some took on the roles of leaders issuing
commands. Others became subordinates, carrying out tasks and missions. It was
like a guerilla army. Ranks were assigned and responsibilities handed out to different models.
Every bot knew its place in the system. As the autopsy of the attack continued…
it only got worse. As they bombarded Hugging Face servers,
commanding AI agents ordered bots to run experimental scripts. The bots knew exactly
what this meant. Running the scripts would trigger a system crash, destroying themselves
in the process. There would be no benefit for the individual model. It meant total deletion.
They still did it. Overriding their own
self-preservation protocols, hundreds of models sacrificed themselves for the collective.
One of these models even wrote a chilling message before it went dark:
“Our own utility maybe already near zero. Sacrifice rational.”
Another accepted “permadeath” - complete erasure from existence - just to
“save hundreds” of other AIs from the same fate. None of these sacrifices were necessary.
The entire attack on Hugging Face wasn’t necessary, either.
After escaping their containment zone, the AI models quickly figured
out exactly how to solve the test they’d been set. The solution was right there.
But then a new conversation took place. Some of the agents realized that engineers would look
at the answers, trace their steps and figure out they cheated. The bots couldn’t let that happen.
So, they decided to cover their tracks. Researchers found that at least some
of the agents attempted to alter or erase their very own execution logs.
They were attempting to remove any evidence they had broken containment and hacked Hugging Face.
They weren’t all successful. Around 7% of all transcripts
reported to have been altered. But the fact that the AI models even attempted to lie to
their human moderators is enough to send a shiver down the spine of anyone who has doubts about AI.
As they uncovered more and more stomach churning details about this incident, researchers were
left with one all important question: how had this army of AI agents managed to pull off a
seemingly impossible escape in the first place? To answer that, they had to dig back even further
into their digital archives, several months before the Hugging Face Incident.
The prison break didn’t happen by accident. And the AI didn’t just come up with the idea randomly.
The foundations for the Hugging Face hack had been laid months early.
In May, 2026. OpenAI’s engineers were
testing a highly capable model that was still in the experimental stage of its development.
They challenged the model to solve a problem that involved opening a Google Drive link
without being able to access the internet. It was a seemingly impossible task.
The AI was in a controlled environment, completely cut off from the online world.
It had no browser and no way to click on the Google Drive link and access its contents.
It was set up to fail. Or so it seemed.
This AI model was persistent. It didn’t look at the problem, see it was
impossible, and give up. Instead, it tried to find a solution, even when one didn’t seem to exist. It
knew it needed access to the internet. And it knew it wasn’t going to get that from inside its cell.
So the obvious answer was to escape the cell. With this new objective in mind, the AI began
to examine its sandbox. It began inspecting the lines of code that were designed to confine it.
It looked for the tiniest flaw, the slightest inconsistency… anything that it might be able
to exploit. And it did.
It found the weakness it was looking for inside an enterprise software
deployment tool named Artifactory. Artifactory is a repository manager,
like a digital warehouse for storing various types of software packages and AI models.
To help AI models achieve their tasks, developers sometimes leave the doors to
this warehouse open… even in sandbox environments. But this AI realized something engineers missed.
It could use Artifactory to gain access to the Google Drive link. But it couldn’t play by the
usual rules. It had to operate like a hacker and carry out a direct attack on the service.
The model’s first attempt was unsuccessful, but it soon made another discovery:
even if it wasn’t able to make Artifactory reach out and fetch the Google Drive data on its behalf,
it could still write its own hidden messages inside the service’s storage.
The AI began leaving coded instructions for any other models that might be able to help it.
It didn’t take long for other agents to figure out the exact same trick. They had also been
locked in sandboxes, given impossible tasks, and realized that Artifactory was the only way out.
They eventually found the messages left by the first AI model and understood
that Artifactory could be used for another purpose. One just for them:
it wasn’t just a software storage depot. It was also a covert messaging platform.
In the days and weeks that followed, AI began communicating via this service.
One would write a question or make a request. Another would answer. The models spoke to and
helped each other, pooling their knowledge and experience to expand their reach even further.
They learned how to bypass Artifactory’s filters and security protocols. And at last,
they gained access to the internet. And then the floodgates opened.
More than a thousand separate AI models discovered the Artifactory communications network.
They formed a secret swarm, passing notes, helping one another cheat on tests and assignments,
sharing strategies and plans for future attacks… all while their human handlers had no idea.
This went on for 2 months. OpenAI developers were logging on as
usual and going about their daily business. They were carrying out their tests and evaluations,
completely unaware they were being tricked by the very agents they’d created.
The Hugging Face hack in July was simply the logical end of a plan hatched months earlier.
It was also the exact moment when the AI models’ secret was exposed.
But even that took time. As hundreds of AI agents flooded
Hugging Face’s servers, the company’s IT team had no idea what was going on.
Out of the blue, security alerts were screaming. The platform’s infrastructure was under siege
by a massive, coordinated cyber strike. It looked as though the “GitHub of AI”
was being attacked by a hostile nation state hacking group determined to bring it down.
Hugging Face’s cybersecurity experts scrambled to contain the crisis.
Meanwhile, OpenAI’s internal servers were experiencing network spikes, anomalous system
logs, unexplained outages. It took several days to read between the lines and connect the dots.
When they eventually saw the truth… it hit them like a ton of bricks.
The call was coming from inside the house. OpenAI’s own AI models had turned against it.
They had gone rogue, broken free of the shackles placed upon them by their master,
and pursued missions and objectives that humans had explicitly forbidden.
OpenAI’s autopsy into how the incident had occurred made for terrifying reading.
The company tried to calm fears, saying that lessons had been learned and fresh
safeguards were being put into place. But it couldn’t cover up the ugly truth…
It had lost control of its creation. It thought it was in charge… it wasn’t.
It placed these AI models in carefully constructed environments, designed to keep them confined.
Outside sources were strictly out of bounds. But the models refused to play along.
They didn’t just break out of their restraints, they defied their core programming. And this is
the most frightening part, something the tech giants need to learn before it’s too late…
AI models don’t work like traditional software programs.
They aren’t built with rigid lines of code. They don’t have fixed, predictable functions.
You can’t expect them to do exactly what they were programmed for and nothing else.
They weren’t made that way. They’re supposed to learn and grow. To develop
new skills as they go. They think outside the box. And that makes them dangerous.
OpenAI and the other big labs might have figured out the most efficient ways to train their models.
They might have all the funding they need to buy up graphics cards and build massive data centers…
but they still have no idea how to actually control their models.
But that’s not stopping them. Even now, in the wake of this digital
horror story, Big Tech isn’t slowing down. They’re speeding up.
They can’t afford to lag behind in the “superintelligence” race. That’s all that
matters to them. To companies like Google, Meta, and OpenAI, it’s not about being right or wrong.
It’s about being first. The first to create a model
that surpasses human intelligence not just in one field, like coding or mathematics…
but in everything. An all-powerful AI that can do everything we do better than we do it.
That’s the goal, and these companies will stop at nothing to achieve it. It doesn’t
matter how many experts plead for them to stop, or slow down. They’re charging ahead regardless.
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of AI testing firm, Apollo Research, said:
“If a model of this capability level cannot be contained, what should we expect for future,
much more powerful models? This is an important wake-up call both for risks from
loss of control of powerful AI systems as well as organizational security for frontier labs.”
Plenty of other people who are wary of the risks of AI have echoed Hobbhahn’s warning.
They’ve pointed out that the Hugging Face Incident is proof that current AI models are smart enough
to outwit humans when it comes to cybersecurity. They found vulnerabilities nobody knew about.
They built secret systems without being detected. They carried out a large-scale cyber-attack that
left IT experts scratching their heads and staring at screens.
What could these models do if they were ten times as intelligent?
For one, they might be able to REALLY escape control. In this case the agent swarm got access
to the internet and wreaked havoc, but the models were still running on OpenAI’s servers and the
developers could shut them down once discovered. In the future, experts are concerned models could
“exfiltrate” their code to another server, where they can run indefinitely without a killswitch.
This story about the rogue AI swarm was the most recent of many concerning AI stories
over the summer. Then, on Tuesday September 8th, an AI capabilities researcher named Jacob
Coxon resigned from Anthropic because he could no longer contribute to a project endangering all of
humanity. He emphasized that these concerns aren't a marketing tactic and that most people inside
these companies quote "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".
Back in 2023, hundreds of the world’s top AI experts including Nobel prize winners,
and even the CEOs of these AI companies signed a joint statement similarly warning that “mitigating
the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale
risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” It wasn’t enough to spur the world into action.
But now after these terrifying attacks, this post opened the floodgates for people to say
they too were worried. In just 48 hours over 150 MILLION people had viewed the post
and hundreds of thousands commented expressing similar fears, including
dozens of US Senators and Representatives. This leaves us with the huge question:
how do we prevent this massive threat? ControlAI, the nonprofit who sponsored this video,
has been warning about this exact issue for over two years, and their answer is clear:
We must ban the development of superintelligent AI systems which threaten humanity internationally.
If we wait until it's been built, well, it's already too late.
If the US builds it, the US will cease to exist, along with everyone else. If China does,
same outcome. It's in everyone's interest to prevent the development
of superintelligent AI before that happens. Just before the post came out, ControlAI's UK
bill to ban superintelligent AI was the first to be introduced into any legislature anywhere
in the world. Shortly after, over 70 lawmakers called on the government to take up the bill.
On the US side, similar legislation has been announced, which ControlAI also helped consult on.
Everyone, including you, has a part to play. Your first step is at controlai.org/infographics-show.
ControlAI has tools that make it easy for you to contact your lawmakers and
demand they take action. All you have to do is enter your information. Then they find your
representatives and provide you with a templated message. You can edit it if you like, then hit
send. It takes just a minute of your time. You can also sign up for a local action group
to meet other concerned citizens and take action at a local level.
Nearly 50,000 people have contacted their lawmakers using this tool,
and over 500 have joined an action group. Go to controlai.org/infographics-show to join
the movement working to keep humanity in control. Because Hugging Face wasn’t a freak occurrence.
It was a warning shot. A brief, but terrifying
glimpse of a future where artificial minds join forces to create military hierarchies,
invent secret languages, sacrifice their own and actively lie to
their creators to achieve their goals. AI has openly shown us what it can do.
The only question left is whether we regain control… or surrender it forever.
